Session consistency is the default and most popular choice — it guarantees monotonic reads, monotonic writes, read-your-writes, and write-follows-reads within a session, covering most application needs without the latency cost of strong consistency.

On the DP-900 exam, map financial/banking scenarios to Strong consistency, globally distributed social media to Eventual, and user-facing applications needing "see your own changes" to Session consistency.

question.title: Azure Cache for Redis
question.scenario: A web application experiences slow performance because it frequently queries the same data from the database. The team wants to store frequently accessed data in memory to reduce database load and improve response times.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides an in-memory data store for caching scenarios?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs an in-memory data store to cache frequently accessed data and reduce database round-trips. Azure offers a managed service based on the widely-used open-source Redis cache.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Cache for Redis (B) is a fully managed in-memory data store based on open-source Redis, designed specifically for caching frequently accessed data to reduce database load and achieve sub-millisecond response times. Azure Cosmos DB (A) is a persistent NoSQL database — while it offers low latency, it is not an in-memory cache and is significantly more expensive for pure caching scenarios. Azure Table Storage (C) stores data on disk, not in memory, and does not provide the sub-millisecond access times needed for caching. Azure Blob Storage (D) is object storage for files and documents, completely unsuited for in-memory data caching.

ul.li: Azure Cache for Redis supports common caching patterns: cache-aside (application checks cache first, falls back to database on miss), write-through (writes go to both cache and database), and write-behind (writes go to cache immediately, asynchronously synced to database).

Beyond simple key-value caching, Redis supports rich data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, and streams — enabling use cases like session state management, real-time leaderboards, rate limiting, and pub/sub messaging.

Azure Cache for Redis offers three tiers: Basic (single node, no SLA — development only), Standard (replicated primary/secondary with SLA), and Premium (clustering, persistence, VNet isolation, geo-replication for enterprise workloads).
On the DP-900 exam, Redis is the answer when the scenario mentions: in-memory, caching, session state, reducing database load, or sub-millisecond latency for repeated data access patterns.

question.title: Azure Synapse Analytics Overview
question.scenario: A company wants to unify their data warehousing and big data analytics on a single platform. They need to perform SQL queries on structured data and Spark-based analytics on large data sets, all within one integrated service.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides a unified analytics platform for data warehousing and big data?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario requires a single platform that unifies SQL-based data warehousing and Spark-based big data analytics. One Azure service is explicitly designed as this unified analytics workspace.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Synapse Analytics (C) is a unified analytics service that combines enterprise data warehousing (dedicated SQL pools), big data analytics (Apache Spark pools), data integration (Synapse pipelines), and serverless SQL queries in a single workspace. Azure Databricks (A) provides Spark-based analytics and ML but is not a data warehouse — it focuses on data engineering and data science, not unified SQL warehousing. Azure HDInsight (B) offers managed open-source clusters (Hadoop, Spark, Kafka) but is not a unified platform — each cluster type is managed separately. Azure Data Factory (D) is a data integration and orchestration service for building ETL/ELT pipelines, not an analytics or warehousing platform.

ul.li: Synapse Analytics has four compute options: Dedicated SQL pools (provisioned MPP data warehouse), Serverless SQL pools (pay-per-query over data lake files), Apache Spark pools (big data processing and ML), and Data Explorer pools (log and telemetry analytics).

Synapse Studio provides a unified web-based workspace for all analytics tasks — SQL development, Spark notebooks, data integration pipelines, monitoring, and Power BI integration, eliminating the need to switch between separate tools.

Synapse integrates natively with Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, allowing serverless SQL to query Parquet, CSV, and JSON files directly in the data lake without loading them into a warehouse — this is a key DP-900 concept called "data lake querying."

On the DP-900 exam, Synapse is the answer when the scenario mentions: unified analytics, combining SQL and Spark, data warehousing with big data, or a single platform for multiple analytics workloads. It is the centerpiece of the modern data warehouse architecture.

question.title: Data Warehouse Concepts
question.scenario: A retail company wants to analyze years of sales data to identify trends across products, stores, and time periods. They need to store historical data from multiple source systems in a way optimized for complex analytical queries and reporting.
question.question-text: What type of data store is specifically designed for this analytical reporting scenario?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs historical data from multiple sources, optimized for complex analytical queries and reporting across dimensions like product, store, and time. This is the textbook definition of one data store type.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A data warehouse (D) is a central repository that consolidates data from multiple source systems, stores it historically, and is optimized for complex analytical queries and reporting — exactly matching the retail scenario. An OLTP database (A) is optimized for fast transactional operations (inserts, updates) with normalized schemas, not for complex analytical queries across years of data. A key-value store (B) provides simple lookups by key and cannot perform the multi-dimensional aggregations needed for trend analysis. A document database (C) stores flexible JSON-like documents and is designed for application data access patterns, not for cross-source historical analytics with complex joins and aggregations.

ul.li: Data warehouses use denormalized schemas (star or snowflake) optimized for read-heavy analytical queries, unlike OLTP databases which use normalized schemas optimized for write-heavy transactional operations. This structural difference is fundamental to the DP-900 exam.

In Azure, data warehouses are implemented using Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools, which use MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) to distribute query execution across multiple compute nodes for fast performance on terabytes of data.

Data warehouses follow the subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, and non-volatile characteristics defined by Bill Inmon — data is organized by business subjects (sales, inventory), integrated from multiple sources, stored with time dimensions, and not modified after loading.

A data mart is a subset of a data warehouse focused on a single department or business line (e.g., a "sales data mart"). On the DP-900 exam, data marts are smaller, focused versions of data warehouses serving specific teams.

question.title: Star Schema Design
question.scenario: A data warehouse architect is designing a schema for sales analysis. They create a central Sales table containing measures like quantity and revenue, surrounded by dimension tables for Product, Customer, Time, and Store that contain descriptive attributes.
question.question-text: What type of data warehouse schema is being described?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A central fact table with measures surrounded by denormalized dimension tables forms a distinctive shape. The visual pattern of one center table with several tables radiating outward gives this schema its name.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A star schema (D) has a central fact table (Sales with measures like quantity and revenue) directly connected to denormalized dimension tables (Product, Customer, Time, Store) — the visual layout resembles a star. A normalized schema (A) applies relational normalization rules (3NF) to eliminate redundancy, which is the opposite of the denormalized dimension tables described here. A snowflake schema (B) is similar to a star but with normalized dimension tables that branch into sub-tables (e.g., Product connects to Category, which connects to Department) — the scenario describes dimensions connected directly to the fact table without further branching. A flat schema (C) is not a recognized data warehouse schema type.

ul.li: Star schema is the most common data warehouse design because it provides fast query performance — queries typically involve one fact table joined to a few dimension tables, and the denormalized dimensions avoid multi-level joins.

Star vs snowflake on the DP-900 exam: star has denormalized dimensions (fewer joins, simpler queries, more storage), snowflake has normalized dimensions (more joins, less redundancy, more complex queries). Star is generally preferred for its simplicity and performance.

Fact tables contain two types of columns: measures (numeric values like revenue, quantity that can be aggregated) and foreign keys that reference dimension tables. Dimension tables contain descriptive attributes (product name, customer city, date components) used for filtering and grouping.

Power BI data models are typically built as star schemas — the Power BI modeling engine (VertiPaq) is optimized for star schema patterns, and Microsoft documentation explicitly recommends star schema as the best practice for Power BI datasets.

question.title: Fact and Dimension Tables
question.scenario: A data warehouse contains a table that stores daily sales transactions with columns for sale amount, quantity sold, and foreign keys to other tables. It contains millions of rows representing measurable business events.
question.question-text: What type of data warehouse table stores measurable business events with numeric values?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The table stores numeric measures (sale amount, quantity) representing business events, contains millions of rows, and has foreign keys to other tables. This is the central, largest table in a data warehouse schema.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A fact table (B) stores quantitative measures (sale amount, quantity sold) about business events along with foreign keys to dimension tables, and typically contains millions to billions of rows — it is the central table in a star or snowflake schema. A dimension table (A) stores descriptive attributes (product name, customer city, date details) used for filtering and grouping, with far fewer rows than fact tables. A lookup table (C) is a general database concept for reference data, not a specific data warehouse term. A bridge table (D) resolves many-to-many relationships between fact and dimension tables — it is a specialized connector, not a primary data store for business events.

ul.li: Fact tables contain three types of measures: additive (can be summed across all dimensions, like revenue), semi-additive (can be summed across some dimensions, like account balance), and non-additive (cannot be summed, like temperature or ratios).

Common fact table types: transaction facts (one row per event, like individual sales), periodic snapshot facts (one row per time period, like daily inventory levels), and accumulating snapshot facts (one row per process, updated as the process progresses, like order fulfillment stages).

The grain of a fact table defines the level of detail — "one row per line item per transaction" is a finer grain than "one row per transaction." Choosing the grain is the most important fact table design decision because it determines what questions the warehouse can answer.

On the DP-900 exam, distinguish fact from dimension by asking: does the column contain numbers you want to sum, average, or count (fact measure)? Or does it contain text you want to filter or group by (dimension attribute)?

question.title: Azure Data Factory Overview
question.scenario: A company needs to orchestrate data movement from multiple sources including on-premises SQL Server, cloud storage, and SaaS applications. They need to schedule data pipelines, transform data, and load it into their data warehouse.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides data integration and orchestration capabilities?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs data pipeline orchestration across on-premises and cloud sources, with scheduling, transformation, and loading. One Azure service is purpose-built for data integration and workflow orchestration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Data Factory (D) is a cloud-based data integration service that creates, schedules, and orchestrates data pipelines — it has 90+ built-in connectors for on-premises and cloud sources, mapping data flows for transformations, and trigger-based scheduling. Azure Synapse Analytics (A) includes pipeline capabilities (inherited from Data Factory) but is primarily an analytics platform, not a standalone integration service — the scenario asks specifically about data movement and orchestration. Azure Databricks (B) provides Spark-based data processing and transformation but is not a pipeline orchestration tool — it processes data but does not manage the end-to-end flow between sources and destinations. Azure Stream Analytics (C) processes real-time streaming data, not scheduled batch pipelines from multiple sources.

ul.li: Azure Data Factory pipelines consist of activities (individual processing steps), datasets (data references), linked services (connection definitions), and triggers (schedule, event, or tumbling window). The visual pipeline designer enables code-free ETL/ELT development.

The Self-Hosted Integration Runtime enables Data Factory to connect to on-premises data sources (SQL Server, file shares, Oracle) securely without opening inbound firewall ports — a critical capability for hybrid cloud data integration.

Data Factory supports two transformation approaches: mapping data flows (code-free visual transformations executed on Spark clusters) and external activities (calling Azure Databricks notebooks, stored procedures, or custom code for complex transformations).

On the DP-900 exam, Data Factory is the answer when the scenario emphasizes: data movement, pipeline orchestration, ETL/ELT, scheduling, multiple data sources, or hybrid (on-premises to cloud) data integration.

question.title: Azure Databricks Overview
question.scenario: A data science team needs a collaborative environment for building machine learning models and performing big data analytics. They prefer using Apache Spark and want interactive notebooks for data exploration and model development.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides a collaborative Apache Spark-based analytics platform?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The team wants Apache Spark with collaborative notebooks for data science and big data analytics. One Azure service is built specifically as a Databricks-managed Spark platform with rich collaboration features.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Databricks (B) is a first-party Azure service built on the Databricks platform, providing optimized Apache Spark clusters, collaborative notebooks (Python, Scala, SQL, R), and an integrated workspace for data engineering and data science. Azure Machine Learning (A) is an MLOps platform for model training, deployment, and management — it focuses on the ML lifecycle, not on Spark-based big data analytics and exploration. Azure HDInsight (C) provides managed open-source clusters including Spark, but it lacks the collaborative notebook workspace and optimization that Databricks provides. Azure Synapse Analytics (D) includes Spark pools but emphasizes unified data warehousing over collaborative data science — its Spark integration is one component of a broader analytics platform.

ul.li: Azure Databricks provides the Databricks Runtime, an optimized version of Apache Spark with performance improvements (Photon engine for SQL queries), Delta Lake integration for reliable data lake operations, and MLflow for experiment tracking and model registry.

Databricks collaborative features include shared notebooks with real-time co-editing, Git integration for version control, job scheduling, cluster management, and Unity Catalog for data governance across the workspace.

Azure Databricks vs Azure Synapse Spark: Databricks is the preferred choice for data science teams needing advanced Spark features, ML workflows, and notebook collaboration. Synapse Spark is better when Spark is one component of a broader warehousing and analytics workflow within Synapse.

On the DP-900 exam, Databricks is the answer when the scenario mentions: Apache Spark, collaborative notebooks, data science workflows, big data analytics with ML, or Databricks by name. It is positioned as the premium Spark platform in Azure.

question.title: Azure Stream Analytics
question.scenario: A manufacturing company needs to analyze sensor data from IoT devices in real-time. They want to detect anomalies as they occur and trigger alerts within seconds of unusual readings being recorded.
question.question-text: Which Azure service is designed for real-time stream processing and analytics?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario requires real-time analysis of IoT sensor data with anomaly detection and alerts within seconds. One Azure service is purpose-built for processing streaming data with SQL-like queries.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Stream Analytics (B) is a real-time analytics service that processes streaming data using SQL-like queries, with built-in anomaly detection, windowing functions, and the ability to trigger alerts within seconds — perfectly matching the IoT manufacturing scenario. Azure Data Factory (A) orchestrates batch data pipelines on schedules, not real-time stream processing. Azure Databricks (C) can process streaming data using Spark Structured Streaming, but it requires more setup and coding and is not the purpose-built, serverless stream processing service described here. Azure Synapse Analytics (D) is primarily for batch analytics and data warehousing, not for sub-second real-time event processing.

ul.li: Azure Stream Analytics uses a SQL-like query language (SAQL) extended with temporal functions — queries like SELECT * FROM SensorInput TIMESTAMP BY EventTime WHERE Temperature > 100 enable declarative real-time filtering without writing imperative code.

Stream Analytics integrates with Azure IoT Hub and Event Hubs as inputs, and can output to Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Blob Storage, Power BI (real-time dashboards), Azure Functions (custom actions), and Service Bus (alerts and notifications).

The built-in anomaly detection functions (AnomalyDetection_SpikeAndDip, AnomalyDetection_ChangePoint) use machine learning models that require no training — they detect spikes, dips, and level changes in streaming data automatically.

On the DP-900 exam, Stream Analytics is the answer for: real-time analytics, IoT data processing, streaming data, sub-second latency requirements, and continuous query processing. It is the managed, serverless option — compare with Spark Structured Streaming on Databricks for more complex streaming scenarios.

question.title: Power BI Overview
question.scenario: A business team needs to create interactive reports and dashboards from their company's data. They want to share visualizations with colleagues and enable self-service analytics for business users without requiring deep technical skills.
question.question-text: Which Microsoft tool provides self-service business intelligence and data visualization?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs interactive reports, dashboards, sharing, and self-service analytics for non-technical business users. Microsoft's flagship BI and visualization tool is designed for exactly this audience.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Power BI (D) is Microsoft's business analytics service that enables business users to create interactive reports and dashboards, share them across the organization, and perform self-service data exploration — all with a drag-and-drop interface requiring no deep technical skills. Azure Synapse Analytics (A) is a data platform for engineers and analysts who write SQL and Spark code, not for self-service business user visualization. Azure Data Factory (B) moves and transforms data in pipelines but has no visualization or reporting capabilities. Azure Analysis Services (C) provides semantic data modeling (tabular models) that Power BI consumes, but it is a backend service without end-user visualization features.

ul.li: Power BI has three components: Power BI Desktop (Windows authoring tool for creating reports), Power BI Service (cloud-based SaaS for publishing, sharing, and collaboration), and Power BI Mobile (iOS/Android apps for consuming reports on the go).

Power BI can connect to hundreds of data sources including Azure SQL, Synapse, Excel, SharePoint, Dynamics 365, Salesforce, and web APIs. Power Query (M language) handles data transformation, and DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) creates calculated measures and columns.

Power BI integrates directly into Azure Synapse Analytics — Synapse Studio includes a Power BI linked service that lets analysts create and view Power BI reports without leaving the Synapse workspace.

On the DP-900 exam, Power BI is always the answer for: data visualization, interactive reports, dashboards, self-service BI, business user analytics, and sharing insights across the organization. It is the final consumption layer in the Azure data analytics pipeline.

question.title: Data Lake Concepts
question.scenario: An organization wants to store all their data - structured, semi-structured, and unstructured - in a central repository in its raw native format. Data scientists and analysts can then process and analyze this data using various tools as needed.
question.question-text: What type of data storage architecture stores data in its raw native format?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario stores all data types (structured, semi-structured, unstructured) in raw native format for later processing. This "store everything raw, process later" approach defines one specific storage architecture.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A data lake (B) stores data in its raw native format — structured, semi-structured, and unstructured — without requiring upfront transformation, enabling schema-on-read where data is interpreted when analyzed rather than when stored. A data warehouse (A) stores transformed, cleansed, structured data in a defined schema (schema-on-write) optimized for specific analytical queries — it does not store raw or unstructured data. A data mart (C) is a focused subset of a data warehouse serving a specific department, even more constrained in scope. An operational database (D) is an OLTP system for recording business transactions, not a central repository for all raw data types.

ul.li: Data lake vs data warehouse on the DP-900 exam: data lakes store raw data with schema-on-read (flexibility, all data types, lower cost), while data warehouses store processed data with schema-on-write (performance, structured only, higher cost). Modern architectures use both.
In Azure, data lakes are built on Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, which provides hierarchical namespace, POSIX ACLs, and integration with Spark, Synapse, and Databricks for processing the raw data.

A common risk with data lakes is becoming a "data swamp" — raw data without proper governance, metadata, and cataloging becomes unusable. Microsoft Purview provides data governance to prevent this by cataloging, classifying, and tracking lineage of data lake contents.

The Medallion architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold layers) is a popular data lake organizational pattern: Bronze stores raw ingested data, Silver stores cleansed and enriched data, and Gold stores curated business-ready data — progressively refining data quality through the layers.

question.title: Azure HDInsight
question.scenario: A company wants to run open-source big data frameworks including Hadoop, Spark, Hive, and Kafka in Azure. They need a managed cluster service that supports these popular open-source analytics technologies.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides managed clusters for popular open-source big data frameworks?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario requires managed clusters for multiple open-source frameworks: Hadoop, Spark, Hive, and Kafka. One Azure service provides managed deployments of these diverse open-source big data technologies.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure HDInsight (B) is a managed cloud service that provides clusters for a broad range of open-source analytics frameworks — Hadoop (MapReduce), Spark, Hive, HBase, Kafka, and Storm — all managed by Azure with automated provisioning and scaling. Azure Databricks (A) provides only Spark (with Databricks optimizations) and does not support Hadoop MapReduce, HBase, Kafka, or the other open-source frameworks mentioned. Azure Synapse Analytics (C) includes Spark pools but not Hadoop, HBase, or Kafka clusters — it is an integrated analytics platform, not a general-purpose open-source cluster service. Azure Data Factory (D) orchestrates data pipelines but does not provide compute clusters for running big data frameworks.

ul.li: HDInsight supports multiple cluster types: Hadoop (batch processing with MapReduce and Hive), Spark (in-memory analytics and ML), HBase (NoSQL column-family database), Kafka (distributed streaming platform), Storm (real-time stream processing), and Interactive Query (LLAP for fast Hive queries).

HDInsight vs Databricks on the DP-900 exam: HDInsight covers the broadest range of open-source frameworks and is best when you need specific technologies like Kafka or HBase. Databricks is preferred when you specifically need optimized Spark with collaborative notebooks and ML workflows.

HDInsight integrates with Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 as its primary storage layer, Azure Monitor for logging and diagnostics, and Azure Active Directory for authentication — enterprise features built on top of open-source distributions.

HDInsight clusters can be created on demand and deleted after processing completes, enabling a pay-for-what-you-use model. This ephemeral cluster pattern is common for batch processing jobs where data persists in ADLS Gen2 between runs.

question.title: Modern Data Warehouse Architecture
question.scenario: An enterprise is designing their analytics architecture. They plan to ingest raw data into a data lake, use data pipelines to transform and load data into a data warehouse, and then serve it to Power BI for visualization.
question.question-text: What is this integrated approach to analytics architecture commonly called?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The architecture described combines a data lake for raw ingestion, pipelines for transformation, a data warehouse for curated storage, and Power BI for visualization. This is the standard Azure reference architecture by a specific name.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A modern data warehouse (B) is Microsoft's reference architecture that integrates a data lake (raw storage), data pipelines (ETL/ELT transformation), a data warehouse (curated analytical storage), and a BI tool like Power BI (visualization) into a cohesive analytics solution — exactly what the scenario describes. A Lambda architecture (A) specifically separates processing into a batch layer and a speed layer for real-time, merging results at a serving layer — the scenario does not describe this dual-path pattern. A Kappa architecture (C) processes all data through a single streaming pipeline, eliminating the batch layer — not matching the described batch-oriented pipeline flow. A Medallion architecture (D) organizes data within a data lake into Bronze/Silver/Gold quality layers — it is a data lake pattern, not the full end-to-end architecture from ingestion through visualization.

ul.li: The modern data warehouse in Azure typically uses: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (raw data lake), Azure Data Factory or Synapse Pipelines (ETL/ELT orchestration), Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools (data warehouse), and Power BI (visualization and reporting).

Azure Synapse Analytics is designed to be the hub of the modern data warehouse architecture — it can serve as both the pipeline orchestrator (Synapse Pipelines) and the warehouse (dedicated SQL pools), with native integration to ADLS Gen2 and Power BI.

The modern data warehouse pattern supports both batch and interactive analytics: batch pipelines load curated data into the warehouse on schedule, while serverless SQL pools enable ad-hoc exploration of raw data lake files without waiting for the ETL to complete.

On the DP-900 exam, the modern data warehouse is the most frequently tested architecture pattern. Know the data flow: sources then data lake (raw) then pipelines (transform) then data warehouse (curated) then Power BI (visualize). Each Azure service maps to one step in this flow.

question.title: Data Visualization Concepts
question.scenario: A sales manager wants to see monthly revenue trends over the past year. They need a visual representation that shows how values change over time with data points connected to show the trend.
question.question-text: Which type of data visualization is best suited for showing trends over time?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs to show how values change over time with connected data points revealing a trend. One chart type is universally associated with displaying trends and continuous data over time.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A line chart (A) connects data points with lines to show trends, patterns, and changes over continuous time intervals — it is the standard visualization for time-series data like monthly revenue. A bar chart (B) compares discrete categories or values using rectangular bars and is better for comparing amounts across categories (e.g., revenue by region) than for showing temporal trends. A pie chart (C) shows proportional composition of a whole (e.g., market share percentages) and cannot effectively display changes over time. A scatter plot (D) shows the relationship between two variables using individual data points without connecting lines — useful for correlation analysis, not temporal trends.

ul.li: In Power BI, line charts can be enhanced with: trend lines (linear, exponential, polynomial regression), forecasting (built-in time-series prediction extending the line into the future), and anomaly detection (automatically highlighting unusual data points).

Visualization selection guide for DP-900: line charts (trends over time), bar/column charts (comparing categories), pie/donut charts (part-to-whole proportions), scatter plots (correlations between two variables), maps (geographic data), and KPI cards (single metrics against targets).

Line charts work best when the x-axis represents continuous, ordered data (typically time). If the x-axis is categorical without inherent order, a bar chart is more appropriate because connecting unrelated categories with lines implies a false trend.

Power BI supports combo charts that overlay line and bar charts — for example, showing monthly revenue as bars with a profit margin trend line overlaid, combining category comparison with trend visualization in a single visual.

question.title: Azure Purview Data Governance
question.scenario: An enterprise needs to create a unified data catalog across their Azure and on-premises data sources. They want to automatically discover and classify sensitive data, track data lineage, and enable business users to find and understand available data assets.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides unified data governance and catalog capabilities?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario requires data cataloging, sensitive data classification, lineage tracking, and data discovery across hybrid environments. One Microsoft service is purpose-built for unified data governance.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Microsoft Purview (A) provides unified data governance with automated data discovery, sensitive data classification (using built-in and custom classifiers), end-to-end data lineage tracking, and a searchable data catalog that helps business users find and understand data assets across Azure, on-premises, and multi-cloud environments. Azure Monitor (B) monitors infrastructure and application performance (metrics, logs, alerts) — it is an observability tool, not a data governance or cataloging service. Azure Synapse Analytics (C) is an analytics platform for querying and processing data, not for cataloging or governing it. Azure Data Factory (D) moves and transforms data in pipelines — while it produces lineage metadata that Purview can consume, it does not provide the catalog, classification, or governance capabilities itself.

ul.li: Microsoft Purview has two main capability areas: Data Governance (data catalog, data map, data lineage, data quality) and Compliance (information protection, data loss prevention, insider risk management, eDiscovery). The DP-900 exam focuses on the data governance side.

Purview automatically scans data sources (Azure SQL, ADLS Gen2, Synapse, Power BI, on-premises SQL Server via self-hosted runtime) and builds a live data map with automatic classification of sensitive data types like SSN, credit card numbers, and email addresses.

Data lineage in Purview shows the end-to-end flow of data from source through transformations to consumption — for example, tracing how raw sales data in ADLS Gen2 flows through Data Factory pipelines into Synapse, then into a Power BI report, answering "where did this number come from?"

On the DP-900 exam, Purview is the answer for: data governance, data catalog, data classification, data lineage, data discovery, and understanding what data exists across the organization. It is the governance layer that sits across the entire data estate.

term.name: Structured Data
term.definition: Data organized in a defined format with fixed schema, typically stored in rows and columns in relational databases.

term.name: Semi-Structured Data
term.definition: Data with some organizational properties like tags or markers but without a rigid schema, such as JSON or XML.

term.name: Unstructured Data
term.definition: Data without a predefined format or organization, such as documents, images, videos, and audio files.

term.name: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)
term.definition: Database systems optimized for managing transaction-oriented applications with many concurrent users performing quick operations.

term.name: OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)
term.definition: Database systems optimized for complex analytical queries, aggregations, and historical data analysis.

term.name: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load)
term.definition: A data integration process that extracts data from sources, transforms it to meet requirements, and loads it into a destination system.

term.name: Data Warehouse
term.definition: A central repository of integrated data from multiple sources, optimized for analytical queries and reporting.

term.name: Data Lake
term.definition: A storage repository that holds vast amounts of raw data in its native format until needed for analysis.

term.name: NoSQL
term.definition: Non-relational databases designed for specific data models with flexible schemas, including document, key-value, column-family, and graph databases.

term.name: Partition Key
term.definition: A value used to distribute data across physical partitions in distributed databases like Cosmos DB for scalability and performance.

term.name: Star Schema
term.definition: A data warehouse schema with a central fact table surrounded by denormalized dimension tables, forming a star pattern.

term.name: Fact Table
term.definition: A table in a data warehouse containing quantitative data (measures) about business events that can be aggregated and analyzed.
